newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Little support for mine shafts as S.African jails.
newsitem.headline: Little support for mine shafts as S.African jails.

text.p: South African prison authorities said on Thursday they were serious about proposals to incarcerate hard-case inmates in disused mine shafts despite suggestions that the idea must be a joke.
"You want a special kind of facility for a very special kind of criminal," Bert Slabbert, spokesman for Correctional Services Minister Sipo Mzimela, said in a telephone interview.
When the idea was first put forward on Tuesday by prisons commissioner Khulekani Sithole, one newspaper greeted the news with the headline: "Is he joking?"
But Slabbert said Mzimela's department was seriously studying the use of underground mine tunnels as super-maximum security jails.

"We're talking about the kind of prisoner that really deserves to go into a super-maximum... Unfortunately there are people in our system who are really beyond any kind of rehabilitation," he said, adding:
South Africa's overcrowded jails, built for 97,000 inmates but now holding about 125,000, are notorious for the ease with which dangerous criminals can escape, often with the help of corrupt guards.
Slabbert said architects and engineers would first have to study whether it would be structurally possible to keep prisoners in mines, which are often subject to rock falls and collapse.
"And then you also have to look at your constitution and bill of rights," he said.
Sithole on Tuesday described the type of convict who would qualify for an underground jail as "animals that must never see sunlight again".
His statement caused a storm of protest from opposition parties, human rights organisations and one group fighting for animal welfare.
Even The Citizen newspaper, which takes a strong no-nonsense stance on crime, was unimpressed.
"We cannot think of a crazier idea," it said in an editorial on Thursday. "It is so repugnant that this country would be condemned by the civilised world."
Earlier this week police released figures showing that reported rapes in South Africa, already the highest in the world, increased again in 1996 but that other violent crimes declined slightly.
Murders fell to 61.1 per 100,000 people in 1996 from 64.6 the year before. Burglaries stayed level but serious assault and illegal possession of firearms crept up.
